b3145687bdea.title: Health workforce (HWF) candidate
b3145687bdea.content: All people engaged in actions whose primary intent is to enhance health. They may be paid staff or volunteers working full-time or part-time in the public and private sectors. They may be delivering health services, managing the services offered by the system, or addressing social determinants of health. That means that the health workforce includes: all personnel trained in health occupations delivering clinical work in health facilities (such as medical doctors, nurses, or dentists); all non health professionals employed in the health sector, public and private, regardless of their occupation (such as managers, ambulance drivers or teachers of health education); and all those whose work supports the delivery of health services, even if they are employed by other sectors or industries (such as cleaning, catering, security or agency staff working in the health sector) . Cited as: Africa Health Workforce Investment Charter: enabling sustainable health workforce invest ments for universal health coverage and health security for the Africa we want. Brazzaville: WHO African Region, 2024.

9426a44f3af0.title: Health workforce registry candidate
9426a44f3af0.content: The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credential, and classification data for all health workers recognised as part of the national health workforce — including licensed or certified professionals employed in both public and private sectors and, where nationally defined and registered, community health workers and other cadres operating in informal or semi-formal capacities. It maintains a standardised, uniquely identified record for each health worker, providing the common reference point against which clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can consistently identify, verify, and classify the people delivering health services. Cited as: DRAFT V1.0 Reference Architecture and Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for the Health Sector: A Digital Transformation Handbook for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H). July 2026 .

81393510bd5e.title: Health workforce observatory candidate
81393510bd5e.content: There is no consensual definition of what an observatory is. There are various ways and means to achieve the same goals and objectives, and no blue-print or “best practice” can be prescribed (Hemmings, Wilkinson 2003). In the social sector, these organizations go beyond observing and analysing; they also pro-actively intervene on the reality, which they monitor. The simple activity of data and information-gathering and dissemination has effects on the reality of the sector and on the actors’ behaviours. HRH observatories are no exception, and in this sense they are rather more like independent policy think-tanks. It is therefore important to note first that there are various “types” of HRH observatory, which take different forms depending on when they were established, by whom, where they are located organizationally, what functions and activities they perform, which resources and funding sources they have, and on the actors involved in their development and management. Table 1 presents that variety of types of observatories according to a number of significant dimensions. Cited as: Human Resources for Health Observatories: Contributing to Evidence-Based Policy Decisions (WHO, 2012) .

86ab640c6330.title: Licensing candidate
86ab640c6330.content: Licensure is a process by which a governmental authority grants permission to an individual practitioner or health care organization to operate or to engage in an occupation or profession. Licensure to individuals is usually granted after some form of examination or proof of education and may be renewed periodically through payment of a fee and/or proof of continuing education or professional competence (11). Cited as: Health labour market analysis guidebook. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021.

40041713d547.title: Health workforce registry candidate
40041713d547.content: "HWR or HRH registry is a 'single authoritative source of health workforce information, that can provide an accurate count of all health care personnel that either has worked or are currently working at national or sub-national levels, including in the private sector'" (World Health Organization. Monitoring the building blocks of health systems: a handbook of indicators and their measurement strategies.) "The HWR does not function in isolation. It is a part of the Human Resource Information System (HRIS) (also called health workforce information system). HRIS is a system that collects, maintains and analyses data on the health workforce. Other components of HRIS are payroll, training, performance management,migration, benefits and retirement components (Fig. 1). The HWR is, however, a central component of the HRIS and provides data on which all the other components depend. e86fcdfac8dc.title: Education and training institution (Health workforce) candidate
e86fcdfac8dc.content: An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. Cited as: National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023.

fd7d527d86e5.content: The structure that allows the services of health workers to be sought (demanded) and offered (supplied). 47a67846f8b7.title: Health workforce registry candidate
47a67846f8b7.content: “Interoperable health professional registers with a clear legal basis underpin workforce intelligence. Effective registers that integrate data from education, licensing and employment systems are essential if countries are to forecast better at the national and regional levels.” (p5) "A health professional register is an official, usually mandatory, system that records information on individuals who are authorized to practise a regulated health profession. Registers are typically maintained by professional regulators or public authorities and contain data such as professional qualifications, scope of practice, licensing status and, depending on the system, information on employment, sector, working hours and location." (p. 23) "Their primary purpose is to support professional regulation and patient safety, but they can also serve as a critical source of workforce intelligence. Health professional registers represent a critical source of high-quality, routinely updated workforce intelligence. They provide a robust empirical foundation for understanding the size, composition, distribution, and activity patterns of the HCWF and can inform a wide range of policy functions, including workforce forecasting and planning, education and training capacity, regulation, distribution and budgeting." p23. Cited as: Joachim M, Kovács E, Cserháti Z, Williams GA, Falkenbach M, Wismar M. Aligning health workforce forecasting and planning with changing care models: the role of integrated data, mixed methods and professional registers. Policy Brief 78 (HEROES Brief 2). Copenhagen: European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies, WHO Regional Office for Europe; 2026 .

8e0949de92d3.title: Dual practice candidate
8e0949de92d3.content: There are several forms of dual practice. Health professionals can work in a public service provision role and another role: (a) outside: in a completely separate private environment; (b) beside: in a private ward or clinic physically associated with a public facility but run as a separate business; (c) within: where private services are offered inside a public facility but outside public service operating hours or space; or (d) integrated: where additional fees are charged for services offered alongside standard public ones, often informally, on the understanding of a faster – or higher-quality – service. Academics and policy-makers typically restrict the term dual practice to category (a), but it is clear that categories (b), (c) and (d) present alternative scenarios for health professionals to combine public and private practice, and supplement public sector salaries; policy-making in this domain should navigate the trade-offs between the objective of retaining personnel while ensuring their commitment to public sector objectives (15) . Cited as: Health labour market analysis guidebook. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021.

2d9ec8956719.title: Health workforce registry candidate
2d9ec8956719.content: "A health worker registry is a centralized listing of health workers within a country. Information contained within a health worker registry most often comes from different health management information systems (HMIS), such as iHRIS, used, for example, by independent organizations, health clinics run by non-state actors or regulatory bodies. These client systems are often organized around specific workflows revolving around human resources (hiring a new health worker, providing a salary bonus, transferring a health worker to a new location), but the health worker registry may contain only specific information about health workers." . Cited as: "WHO Minimum Data Set (MDS) Crosswalk" — guidance document/tool for mapping the WHO Minimum Data Set to local data elements and vice versa, for use in implementing a health worker registry (undated).

24e5c928a1e9.title: Health workforce registry candidate
24e5c928a1e9.content: Glossary: "Health Worker Registry: a national authority of health worker information according to a defined minimum data set." "Provider Registry: Another synonym for Health Worker Registry." "Health Worker Directory: List of health workers that are managed by individual organizations, which can come together to form a health worker registry." Narrative definition: "A Health Worker Registry (HWR) serves as the digital, central authority for maintaining the unique virtual identities of health workers within a country. The Health Worker Registry pulls data from underlying human resource information systems (HRIS), which play the role of Health Worker Directories, and makes these data available as a single virtual database. These Health Worker Directories could include Ministry of Health installations of tools like iHRIS, private systems used by faith-based organizations, and private-sector systems as well as those used by regulatory bodies like nursing councils. These health Worker directories are responsible for specific business processes: maybe one tracks health worker certifications for a professional council or another holds salary information for the ministry of health. The information stored in these directories mirrors their business cases. The Health Worker Registry has no business case other than being a master document of all health worker information that specific directories can pull and share. The Health Worker Registry contains a Minimum Data Set (MDS) of details of all health workers working in both public and private sectors, such as full name, contact information and place(s) of employment. The Health Worker Registry (HWR) serves as the authority for maintaining the unique identities of health workers within a country (p12) Governments collect and store multiple and disparate sources of data on health workers. Thus, it is a complex task to pull together and maintain a master list of all health workers in a country. A Health Worker Registry (HWR) seeks to reduce the complexity of this task by: ● creating a Minimum Data Set (MDS) of health workforce information from the various source data systems ● merging the information from a variety of data systems into an authoritative registry of health workers according to a data governance policy ● allowing queries of health worker information by various computer and human users, also called the client systems. The HWR serves as a publicly available “electronic phone-book” of health workers and health services across all sectors (public, private and faith-based organizations). As the World Health Organization points out, the HWR can be seen as the “single authoritative source” of health workforce information that parts of the HIS can query to obtain details on health workers and automatically populate their databases, rather than having to manually enter those details themselves. Cited as: "OpenHIE Health Worker Registry (HWR) Implementation Guide" (IntraHealth International/CapacityPlus, 2016 revision).

cb2a4cfcb7b4.title: Health workforce registry candidate
cb2a4cfcb7b4.content: The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credential, and classification data for all health workers recognised as part of the national health workforce — including licensed or certified professionals employed in both public and private sectors and, where nationally defined and registered, community health workers and other cadres operating in informal or semi-formal capacities. It maintains a standardised, uniquely identified record for each health worker, providing the common reference point against which clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can consistently identify, verify, and classify the people delivering health services. The registry holds two interlocking categories of information: 1. The first is identity: who the health worker is — their demographics, unique identifier, and may cross-reference to foundational identification systems. 2. The second is credentials: what the health worker is qualified and authorised to do — their 240 occupational classification, professional registration, licensing status, and qualifications. Together, these form the data foundation for a health system that can assure the quality and accountability of its workforce at scale. The WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) handbook (Second Edition, 2023) defines 29 244 indicators that underpin health workforce monitoring, planning, and policy — covering stock, flow, education, migration, and expenditure. The national health workforce registry is a key data source for 12 of 246 these indicators, notably those measuring stock and flow – critical to workforce planning and equitable distribution. The Health Workforce Registry, as defined in the DPI-H reference architecture, provides the foundational data infrastructure from which these indicators can be derived. Architecture placement: The Health Workforce Registry is a core DPI-H foundational component — the shared identity and credential anchor for health workers across the health ecosystem. It is architecturally distinct from two operational systems: the Human Resources Information System (HRIS), which manages employment transactions, payroll processing, leave management, and workforce scheduling; and the Learning Management System (LMS), which manages training delivery, course enrolment, and assessment. The Health Workforce Registry holds the authoritative master record of who a health worker is and what they are qualified and licensed to do. The HRIS and LMS consume this registry as their reference source; neither replaces it. Cited as: DRAFT V1.0 Reference Architecture and Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for the Health Sector: A Digital Transformation Handbook for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H). July 2026 .

1d96f44fda5e.title: Health workforce registry candidate
1d96f44fda5e.content: "In a national context an electronic health workforce registry can be considered the single authoritative source of health workforce information that can provide an accurate count of all health care personnel that either have worked or are currently working at national or sub-national levels, including in the private sector. An electronic health workforce registry can be designed to authenticate and validate the existence of a health worker and provide essential details about that person." (p. 7) The health workforce registry is a central and essential component of a functional HRIS, as it contains important health worker attributes that can subsequently be linked to other relevant HRIS components." (p8) "In this document, a minimum data set is proposed to construct an electronic health workforce registry. Using this tool, data elements can be standardized within electronic systems to help facilitate the collection, collation, analysis, reporting and utilization of national and sub-national health workforce data. The tool can also assist in achieving data interoperability between and within information systems."(p8) . Cited as: Human Resources for Health Information System: Minimum Data Set for Health Workforce Registry. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2015.

a5b3178493e1.title: Health workforce registry candidate
a5b3178493e1.content: “Regulators generally maintain a registry of regulated practitioners to keep the public informed of those authorized as competent to practice and those who have been suspended or removed from the registry. The level of detail available about practitioners through the regulator’s public website varies between regulators, occupations and countries, from a simple verification of registration to details on qualification, and practice and disciplinary history. Different types of registration exist (for example, student, temporary, provisional, limited practice, supervised practice, private practice, public sector practice, independent practice, specialized practice and nonclinical practice). These determine where a health practitioner can work, their scope of work and level of independence. While in some countries periodic renewals are required to maintain a practitioner’s registration or licence, in others, regulators have limited capacity to maintain a complete registry (p11) Based on data available from regulators, the registries of regulated health practitioners may include information on the number of students in health occupations, active and inactive health practitioners, their personal details, place of education and employment, and the jurisdiction of registration within a country. (p13) The inclusion of disciplinary history in public registries can help patients, clients and employers to make informed choices about practitioners. Regulators can use the data to identify and reduce the risk of harm to the public through preventative action or early identification and intervention (p45) A core function of regulators is to maintain a publicly available registry on regulated health practitioners that is accurate, complete and includes information on practitioners who have been removed from the registry. This enables access to information on practitioners by both the public seeking services and employers recruiting the practitioners. Depending on the occupation and jurisdiction, the information in the public registry can vary. The health practitioner registry accessible to the public is in compliance with legislation and requirements on confidentiality and the handling of personal data and generally includes relevant information on the practitioners such as name, gender, age, registration number, qualification details (such as basic and additional qualifications, conferring institution, year conferred), scope of registration or licensure, disciplinary history and associated sanctions and actions (26, 115, 286–288). Since maintaining an up-to-date public registry has resource implications, the costs and benefits should be assessed for each data point included in the register. Information shared in the public registry is only a subset of the information that is collected by the regulators. Additional information captured by regulators could include practitioner characteristics such as language skills, country of birth, nationality, details on practice location, criminal history records, fitness to practice, and complaints and disciplinary actions. Information on employers may also be captured (26, 289–292). Some of the information held by regulators is confidential and the grounds on which this information may be shared and with whom need to be specified by law. Similarly, the regulator for health practitioner education could hold information on the capacity of the institutions as well as annual data on enrolments and graduates (if applicable) in different programmes, including gender, age, country of birth and the nationality of students. Where assessments of practitioner performance standards are regular and linked to periodic registration or licensure renewals, it can help to keep the practitioner registry updated. In such cases, the available data (for example, on education, entry to practice, maintenance of standards, complaints and discipline) should be analysed to detect clinical governance failures that harm patients, identify innovations and generate evidence and data for improving regulatory systems, practice environments, service delivery and patient safety (p46) . Cited as: World Health Organization. Health Practitioner Regulation: Design, Reform and Implementation Guidance. Geneva: WHO; 2024.

1d678f7c6ac8.doc: Employment status: full-time, part-time, temporary, permanent
1d678f7c6ac8.title: Employment status: full-time, part-time, temporary, permanent candidate
1d678f7c6ac8.content: Full-time (whole-time) is employment for or working for the amount of time considered customary or standard. Part-time is employment for or working for less than the amount of time considered customary or standard. Permanent is employment contracted for an indeterminate period. Fixed term is employment contracted for a fixed period of time. Temporary refers to short-term contracts or “casual” work, either for a definite period or for a specific activity. Self-employment is when remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced by the individual. Cited as: Health labour market analysis guidebook. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021.

0fcd3e734ef3.title: Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) (AFR / South Africa) candidate
0fcd3e734ef3.content: A statutory health regulatory body and a juristic person established under Section 2 of the Health Professions Act (Act No. 56 of 1974). Also called: HPCSA . Regulates: Medicine and 11 other health professions (nursing and pharmacy are regulated separately by their own statutory councils). Mandate: Controls education, training, and registration for health professions; ensures practitioners maintain professional ethics; enforces compulsory Continuing Professional Development (CPD). Reference: Health Professions Act, 1974 (Act No. 56 of 1974) Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Suspected issues, to confirm: No fetch possible. The statute (s.2, Act 56 of 1974) is consistent with the snippets. Likely error in 'professions': the HPCSA has 12 professional boards, one of them the Medical and Dental board, and these cover many more than '11 other health professions'. Board count is not the same as profession count, so rephrase, for example 'medicine, dentistry and other health professions under 12 professional boards'. No URL is given; add the acts.co.za section 2 text or the HPCSA site. f673b0b19b71.title: Federation of State Medical Boards (FSMB) (AMR / United States) candidate
f673b0b19b71.content: A non-profit national coordinating organization for the ~70 state and territorial medical boards that hold the actual statutory licensing authority for physicians in the United States (there is no single federal medical licensing body, mirroring NCSBN's role for nursing). Also called: FSMB, USMLE . Regulates: Medicine (coordinating body; actual licensure is issued by individual state medical boards, not FSMB itself). Mandate: Supports state medical boards with shared services, data, and technology (e.g. co-develops the USMLE Step 3 exam with the National Board of Medical Examiners, credentials verification, uniform applications); promotes regulatory best practice and information-sharing among state boards; does not itself register or license physicians. ea24ab59fe76.content: The statutory regulator for doctors (and, since 2024, physician associates and anaesthesia associates) in the UK, operating under the Medical Act 1983 as amended, most recently by the Anaesthesia Associates and Physician Associates Order 2024. 8861f5872963.title: Pakistan Nursing Council (PNC) / Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council (PNMC) (EMR / Pakistan) candidate

703a4e38e370.content: The statutory National Board responsible for regulating the medical profession in Australia, operating under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (2009) as part of Ahpra's National Registration and Accreditation Scheme. Also called: MBA . Regulates: Medicine. Reference: Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009; www.medicalboard.gov.au/; www.ahpra.gov.au/ Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Suspected issues, to confirm: Leads are consistent with the mandate. The statute is the National Law set out in the Schedule to the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009 (Qld) (Act 45 of 2009), adopted by each state and territory; the citation should make clear it is the Queensland host Act. The registration-types list could not be checked. Neither reference URL was reachable. Search leads: www.directory.gov.au/portfolios/health/medical-board-australia, www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/pdf/inforce/2026-04-10/act-2009-045.

dbeb268af60f.content: A statutory body established by the Nurses Act, Chapter 257 of the Laws of Kenya, functioning as the sole professional regulator for nursing and midwifery cadres in Kenya, distinct from the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council. Also called: NCK . Regulates: Nursing and midwifery. Mandate: Registers and licenses nurses and midwives trained domestically or internationally; conducts national licensing examinations; maintains official registers; approves training institutions and curricula; conducts disciplinary proceedings and advises government on nursing matters. f163280845e0.title: Dubai Health Authority (DHA) (EMR / United Arab Emirates (Dubai)) candidate
f163280845e0.content: A public authority with independent legal personality established under Law No. (6) of 2018 Concerning the Dubai Health Authority (superseding the 2007 law that first created it); one of three UAE healthcare regulators alongside the federal Ministry of Health and Prevention (MOHAP, Northern Emirates) and the Abu Dhabi Department of Health (DoH) — the UAE has no single national medical or nursing council, and DHA licenses both doctors and nurses as a single omnibus regulator for Dubai. Also called: DHA, MOHAP, DoH . Regulates: All licensed health professions, including medicine and nursing (single omnibus regulator for Dubai). Mandate: Authorises individuals and facilities to practise health professions in Dubai and issues professional licences; sets bylaws, standards and requirements for practice; audits and inspects practitioners and facilities for compliance; investigates complaints and alleged malpractice. Reference: Law No. (6) of 2018 Concerning the Dubai Health Authority; dlp.dubai.gov.ae/Legislation%20Reference/2018/Law%20No.%20(6)%20of%202018%20Concerning%20the%20Dubai%20Health%20Authority.html; alkabban.com/medical-law/healthcare-regulatory-authorities-uae/ Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Suspected issues, to confirm: Gulf News cites it as Law No. 8 - official portal title confirms No. 6. 04b10a2eb522.title: Federal Council of Nursing (Conselho Federal de Enfermagem - COFEN) (AMR / Brazil) candidate

2982e3c8653c.title: Egyptian Medical Syndicate (EMS) (EMR / Egypt) candidate
2982e3c8653c.content: A semi-governmental professional syndicate founded in 1940, with mandatory membership required for physicians to practise. Sources consulted give conflicting founding/governing law numbers, so the precise statutory citation should be confirmed against the Egyptian Official Gazette before use in the handbook. (Nursing is regulated separately by its own syndicate — see the row added below.) . Also called: EMS . Regulates: Medicine. Mandate: Assists the Ministry of Health in conferring licences to physicians; verifies academic credentials on application and issues practice certificates; administers licence renewals and approval of foreign-trained doctors; since February 2021 shares national licensing-exam administration with the newly created Egyptian Health Council for new graduates. Reference: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Medical_Syndicate; grokipedia.com/page/egyptian_medical_syndicate (law citation unverified — flagged) Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Suspected issues, to confirm: Law 45/1969 number from Arabic legal database manshurat.org, not the Official Gazette. 6d0beae44ccb.title: Lebanese Order of Physicians (LOP) (EMR / Lebanon) candidate
6d0beae44ccb.content: The statutory professional order for physicians in Lebanon, operating under Law No. 1658 of 17 January 1979 regulating the practice of the medical profession (Official Gazette, Issue 10, 8 March 1979). (Nursing is regulated separately — see the Order of Nurses in Lebanon row added below.) . Also called: LOP . Regulates: Medicine. Mandate: Determines physicians' professional eligibility to practise medicine; disciplines members against professional and ethical rules; advises government ministries on health-workforce laws and regulations; administers retirement and welfare funds for members. Reference: Law No. 1658 (1979); lopbeirut.org/en/law-regulating-the-practice-of-the-medical-profession-in-lebanon/; lopbeirut.org/en/lop-role/ Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). 3ad4a1f4c915.doc: Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI)
3ad4a1f4c915.title: Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) (EUR / Ireland) candidate
3ad4a1f4c915.content: The statutory regulatory body for nurses and midwives in Ireland, governed by the Nurses and Midwives Act 2011. Also called: NMBI . Regulates: Nursing and midwifery. Mandate: Protects the public and the integrity of the nursing and midwifery professions; maintains the Register of Nurses and Midwives and a Candidate Register for students; sets standards for and approves education/training programmes; investigates fitness-to-practise complaints and imposes sanctions; advises the Minister for Health on nursing/midwifery matters. Reference: Nurses and Midwives Act 2011 Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Suspected issues, to confirm: Statutory name is Bord Altranais agus Cnáimhseachais na hÉireann (NMBI is the operating name) - not confirmed by fetch. Ministerial-advice function not checked. fdc16f62721a.title: Nursing Board Malaysia (Lembaga Jururawat Malaysia) (WPR / Malaysia) candidate
fdc16f62721a.content: Malaysia's statutory nursing regulator, established under the Nurses Act 1950 and the Nurses Registration Regulations 1985, operating under the Ministry of Health alongside the separate Malaysian Medical Council. Regulates: Nursing (a separate Midwives Board regulates midwifery under the Midwives Act 1966). Mandate: Keeps and maintains the Register of Nurses; regulates nursing practice and training/examination procedures; issues registration credentials; enforces professional conduct standards through an established code of ethics. Reference: Nurses Act 1950; hq.moh.gov.my/nursing/en/about-us/midwives-board/ Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Suspected issues, to confirm: Leads support the Nurses Act 1950 (Act 14) and the Nurses Registration Regulations 1985; give the Act number. The reference URL is the Midwives Board page, not the Nursing Board page, so it is probably the wrong page; the lead suggests hq.moh.gov.my/nursing/?p=3322 (Nursing & Midwives Board). The MOH page reportedly says the nurses/midwives legislation is under review. Search leads: hq.moh.gov.my/nursing/?p=3322, hq.moh.gov.my/nursing/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/2.-NURSES-ACT-1950-2.pdf, www.moh.gov.my/images/04-penerbitan/akta-kesihatan/midviwes act 1966.pdf.

Active health worker candidate One who provides services to patients and communities (practising health worker) or whose medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of the job (e.g. education, research, public administration) even if the health worker is not directly providing services (professionally active health worker). If data are not available for practising or professionally active health workers, data with the closest definition can be used, such as “health worker licensed to practice”. Categories of level are based on the definitions of OECD/Eurostat/WHO-Europe Joint questionnaire on nonmonetary health care statistics. Cited as: National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. Dual practice candidate There are several forms of dual practice. Health professionals can work in a public service provision role and another role: (a) outside: in a completely separate private environment; (b) beside: in a private ward or clinic physically associated with a public facility but run as a separate business; (c) within: where private services are offered inside a public facility but outside public service operating hours or space; or (d) integrated: where additional fees are charged for services offered alongside standard public ones, often informally, on the understanding of a faster – or higher-quality – service. Academics and policy-makers typically restrict the term dual practice to category (a), but it is clear that categories (b), (c) and (d) present alternative scenarios for health professionals to combine public and private practice, and supplement public sector salaries; policy-making in this domain should navigate the trade-offs between the objective of retaining personnel while ensuring their commitment to public sector objectives (15) . Cited as: Health labour market analysis guidebook. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021. Education and training institution (Health workforce) candidate An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. Cited as: National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023. Employment status: full-time, part-time, temporary, permanent candidate Full-time (whole-time) is employment for or working for the amount of time considered customary or standard. Part-time is employment for or working for less than the amount of time considered customary or standard. Permanent is employment contracted for an indeterminate period. Fixed term is employment contracted for a fixed period of time. Temporary refers to short-term contracts or “casual” work, either for a definite period or for a specific activity. Self-employment is when remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced by the individual. Cited as: Health labour market analysis guidebook. Health workforce observatory candidate There is no consensual definition of what an observatory is. There are various ways and means to achieve the same goals and objectives, and no blue-print or “best practice” can be prescribed (Hemmings, Wilkinson 2003). In the social sector, these organizations go beyond observing and analysing; they also pro-actively intervene on the reality, which they monitor. The simple activity of data and information-gathering and dissemination has effects on the reality of the sector and on the actors’ behaviours. HRH observatories are no exception, and in this sense they are rather more like independent policy think-tanks. It is therefore important to note first that there are various “types” of HRH observatory, which take different forms depending on when they were established, by whom, where they are located organizationally, what functions and activities they perform, which resources and funding sources they have, and on the actors involved in their development and management. Table 1 presents that variety of types of observatories according to a number of significant dimensions. Health workforce registry candidate Glossary: "Health Worker Registry: a national authority of health worker information according to a defined minimum data set." "Provider Registry: Another synonym for Health Worker Registry." "Health Worker Directory: List of health workers that are managed by individual organizations, which can come together to form a health worker registry." Narrative definition: "A Health Worker Registry (HWR) serves as the digital, central authority for maintaining the unique virtual identities of health workers within a country. The Health Worker Registry pulls data from underlying human resource information systems (HRIS), which play the role of Health Worker Directories, and makes these data available as a single virtual database. These Health Worker Directories could include Ministry of Health installations of tools like iHRIS, private systems used by faith-based organizations, and private-sector systems as well as those used by regulatory bodies like nursing councils. These health Worker directories are responsible for specific business processes: maybe one tracks health worker certifications for a professional council or another holds salary information for the ministry of health. The information stored in these directories mirrors their business cases. The Health Worker Registry has no business case other than being a master document of all health worker information that specific directories can pull and share. The Health Worker Registry contains a Minimum Data Set (MDS) of details of all health workers working in both public and private sectors, such as full name, contact information and place(s) of employment. The Health Worker Registry (HWR) serves as the authority for maintaining the unique identities of health workers within a country (p12) Governments collect and store multiple and disparate sources of data on health workers. Thus, it is a complex task to pull together and maintain a master list of all health workers in a country. A Health Worker Registry (HWR) seeks to reduce the complexity of this task by: ● creating a Minimum Data Set (MDS) of health workforce information from the various source data systems ● merging the information from a variety of data systems into an authoritative registry of health workers according to a data governance policy ● allowing queries of health worker information by various computer and human users, also called the client systems. The HWR serves as a publicly available “electronic phone-book” of health workers and health services across all sectors (public, private and faith-based organizations). As the World Health Organization points out, the HWR can be seen as the “single authoritative source” of health workforce information that parts of the HIS can query to obtain details on health workers and automatically populate their databases, rather than having to manually enter those details themselves. Cited as: "OpenHIE Health Worker Registry (HWR) Implementation Guide" (IntraHealth International/CapacityPlus, 2016 revision). Health workforce registry candidate “Regulators generally maintain a registry of regulated practitioners to keep the public informed of those authorized as competent to practice and those who have been suspended or removed from the registry. The level of detail available about practitioners through the regulator’s public website varies between regulators, occupations and countries, from a simple verification of registration to details on qualification, and practice and disciplinary history. Different types of registration exist (for example, student, temporary, provisional, limited practice, supervised practice, private practice, public sector practice, independent practice, specialized practice and nonclinical practice). These determine where a health practitioner can work, their scope of work and level of independence. While in some countries periodic renewals are required to maintain a practitioner’s registration or licence, in others, regulators have limited capacity to maintain a complete registry (p11) Based on data available from regulators, the registries of regulated health practitioners may include information on the number of students in health occupations, active and inactive health practitioners, their personal details, place of education and employment, and the jurisdiction of registration within a country. (p13) The inclusion of disciplinary history in public registries can help patients, clients and employers to make informed choices about practitioners. Regulators can use the data to identify and reduce the risk of harm to the public through preventative action or early identification and intervention (p45) A core function of regulators is to maintain a publicly available registry on regulated health practitioners that is accurate, complete and includes information on practitioners who have been removed from the registry. This enables access to information on practitioners by both the public seeking services and employers recruiting the practitioners. Depending on the occupation and jurisdiction, the information in the public registry can vary. The health practitioner registry accessible to the public is in compliance with legislation and requirements on confidentiality and the handling of personal data and generally includes relevant information on the practitioners such as name, gender, age, registration number, qualification details (such as basic and additional qualifications, conferring institution, year conferred), scope of registration or licensure, disciplinary history and associated sanctions and actions (26, 115, 286–288). Since maintaining an up-to-date public registry has resource implications, the costs and benefits should be assessed for each data point included in the register. Information shared in the public registry is only a subset of the information that is collected by the regulators. Additional information captured by regulators could include practitioner characteristics such as language skills, country of birth, nationality, details on practice location, criminal history records, fitness to practice, and complaints and disciplinary actions. Information on employers may also be captured (26, 289–292). Some of the information held by regulators is confidential and the grounds on which this information may be shared and with whom need to be specified by law. Similarly, the regulator for health practitioner education could hold information on the capacity of the institutions as well as annual data on enrolments and graduates (if applicable) in different programmes, including gender, age, country of birth and the nationality of students. Where assessments of practitioner performance standards are regular and linked to periodic registration or licensure renewals, it can help to keep the practitioner registry updated. In such cases, the available data (for example, on education, entry to practice, maintenance of standards, complaints and discipline) should be analysed to detect clinical governance failures that harm patients, identify innovations and generate evidence and data for improving regulatory systems, practice environments, service delivery and patient safety (p46) . Health workforce registry candidate The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credential, and classification data for all health workers recognised as part of the national health workforce — including licensed or certified professionals employed in both public and private sectors and, where nationally defined and registered, community health workers and other cadres operating in informal or semi-formal capacities. It maintains a standardised, uniquely identified record for each health worker, providing the common reference point against which clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can consistently identify, verify, and classify the people delivering health services. The registry holds two interlocking categories of information: 1. The first is identity: who the health worker is — their demographics, unique identifier, and may cross-reference to foundational identification systems. 2. The second is credentials: what the health worker is qualified and authorised to do — their 240 occupational classification, professional registration, licensing status, and qualifications. Together, these form the data foundation for a health system that can assure the quality and accountability of its workforce at scale. The WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) handbook (Second Edition, 2023) defines 29 244 indicators that underpin health workforce monitoring, planning, and policy — covering stock, flow, education, migration, and expenditure. The national health workforce registry is a key data source for 12 of 246 these indicators, notably those measuring stock and flow – critical to workforce planning and equitable distribution. The Health Workforce Registry, as defined in the DPI-H reference architecture, provides the foundational data infrastructure from which these indicators can be derived. Architecture placement: The Health Workforce Registry is a core DPI-H foundational component — the shared identity and credential anchor for health workers across the health ecosystem. It is architecturally distinct from two operational systems: the Human Resources Information System (HRIS), which manages employment transactions, payroll processing, leave management, and workforce scheduling; and the Learning Management System (LMS), which manages training delivery, course enrolment, and assessment. The Health Workforce Registry holds the authoritative master record of who a health worker is and what they are qualified and licensed to do. The HRIS and LMS consume this registry as their reference source; neither replaces it. Cited as: DRAFT V1.0 Reference Architecture and Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for the Health Sector: A Digital Transformation Handbook for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H). Regulates: Nursing. Mandate: Registers nurses and sets standards for nursing education, competence and practice; issues annual practising certificates; investigates fitness-to-practise concerns, in parallel with the Medical Council of New Zealand's equivalent role for doctors. The National Health Workforce Accounts covers health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. 144d571056be.content: Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) EMR / Pakistan candidate The statutory regulatory authority maintaining the official register of medical and dental practitioners in Pakistan, most recently re-established under the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council Act, 2022, after a 2019-2023 period during which its functions were held by the short-lived Pakistan Medical Commission. (Nursing is regulated separately — see the Pakistan Nursing Council row added below.) . Regulates: Medicine and dentistry. Mandate: Sets minimum qualification and education standards for medicine and dentistry jointly with the Higher Education Commission; requires registration of all practitioners and students before legal practice; administers the national licensing/registration examination and register. Reference: Pakistan Medical and Dental Council Act, 2022; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Medical_and_Dental_Council; pmdc.pk/Documents/law/PMDC%20Act.pdf Checked 2026-10-14: not verified (source pages could not be opened; web search only). Professional council candidate Organization with the legal authority to regulate one or more health occupations with a view to protecting the public. Its mandate can cover the regulation of entry into the occupation (education requirements), the monitoring and promotion of the quality of practice, and administration of discipline... At national level (and at subnational level where legislative power exists), examples of mandatory rules are professional laws that define the powers and duties of professional councils, such as registration, certification of specialties and discipline. ad8324a0fe70.content: Saudi Commission for Health Specialties (SCFHS) EMR / Saudi Arabia candidate A Saudi professional scientific commission with an independent legal personality, established by Royal Order No. M/2 of 1992 and supervised by a Board of Trustees; functions as a single omnibus regulator covering medicine, nursing, and other health professions rather than separate profession-specific councils. df257caa1c31.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
df257caa1c31.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 4 | 212 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 216 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.
